Partite saturation number of cycles

Yiduo Xu ††thanks: E-mail:xyd23@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China    Zhen He ††thanks: Corresponding author. E-mail:zhenhe@bjtu.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Beijing Jiaotong University, Beijing 100091, China    Mei Lu ††thanks: E-mail:lumei@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
Abstract

A graph HH is said to be FF-saturated relative to GG, if HH does not contain any copy of FF but the addition of any edge ee in E⁡(G)\E⁡(H)E(G)\backslash E(H) would create a copy of FF. The minimum size of a FF-saturated graph relative to GG is denoted by s​a​t​(G,F)sat(G,F). We use s​a​t​(n,k,F)sat(n,k,F) to denote the partite saturation number s​a​t​(Kk×n,F)sat(K_{k\times n},F), where Kk×nK_{k\times n} is the complete kk-partite graph with nn vertices in each part. In this paper we prove that s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)=k​n+O⁡(ℓ2)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1})=kn+O(\ell^{2}) holds for all ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3, and s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)=k​n+O⁡(ℓ)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1})=kn+O(\ell) holds for ℓ≥60​k+11\ell\geq 60k+11. Also we determine the exact value of s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1}) for all 4≥ℓ≥k≥34\geq\ell\geq k\geq 3.

Keywords. saturation number, saturation graph, partite graph

1 Introduction

In this paper we only consider finite, simple and undirected graphs. For a graph GG, we use V⁡(G)V(G) to denote the vertex set of GG, E⁡(G)E(G) the edge set of GG, |G||G| the order of GG and e⁡(G)e(G) the size of GG. For a positive integer kk, let [k]:={1,2,…,k}[k]:=\{1,2,\ldots,k\}. We say a graph GG is a kk-partite graph, if V⁡(G)V(G) can be partition into kk parts V1,…,VkV_{1},\ldots,V_{k} such that each of ViV_{i} is an independent set ( i.e. for any different u,v∈Viu,v\in V_{i}, u​v∉E⁡(G)uv\not\in E(G)). For a kk-partite graph GG, we simply write G=V1∪V2∪⋯∪VkG=V_{1}\cup V_{2}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k}, where ViV_{i} is the ii-th part of GG. Still we abbreviate GG as bipartite if k=2k=2, tripartite if k=3k=3 and multipartite if k≥3k\geq 3. Denote by Ck,PkC_{k},P_{k} the kk-vertices cycle and path, respectively. The length of a path (cycle) is the edge number of the path (cycle). The girth of a graph GG is the minimum length of cycles in GG.

For graphs G1,G2G_{1},G_{2}, we simply write G1⊆G2G_{1}\subseteq G_{2} (resp. G1⊈G2G_{1}\not\subseteq G_{2}) if G1G_{1} is the subgraph of G2G_{2} (resp. G1G_{1} is not the subgraph of G2G_{2}). For a graph GG and e∉E⁡(G)e\not\in E(G), we use G+eG+e to denote the graph obtained by adding the edge ee into GG. Similarly, given a graph GG and u∈V⁡(G),e∈E⁡(G)u\in V(G),e\in E(G), let G−uG-u (resp. G−eG-e) be the graph obtained by deleting the vertex uu and all edges relating to uu (resp. deleting the edge ee) in GG. For a vertex set (resp. an edge set) AA, let G⁡[A]G[A] be the subgraph of GG induced by AA.

For a graph GG and u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G), let NG​(u)={v:u​v∈E⁡(G)}N_{G}(u)=\{v:uv\in E(G)\} be the neighbourhood of uu, and dG​(u)=|NG​(u)|d_{G}(u)=|N_{G}(u)| the degree of uu. We use δ⁡(G)\delta(G) to denote the minimum degree of GG. Without confusion, we abbreviate as N⁡(u)N(u), d⁡(u)d(u) and δ\delta, respectively. For a vertex set AA, let N⁡(A)=⋃u∈AN⁡(u)∖AN(A)=\bigcup\limits_{u\in A}N(u)\,\setminus\,A. Let N⁡[u]=N⁡(u)∪{u}N[u]=N(u)\cup\{u\} and N⁡[A]=N⁡(A)∪AN[A]=N(A)\cup A. If GG is a partite graph, let Ni​(u)=N⁡(u)∩ViN_{i}(u)=N(u)\cap V_{i} and Ni​(A)=N⁡(A)∩ViN_{i}(A)=N(A)\cap V_{i}. The distance d⁡(u,v)d(u,v) between two vertices u,vu,v is the number of edges contained in the shortest path connecting uu and vv. If u,vu,v are not in the same connected components, then d⁡(u,v)=∞d(u,v)=\infty. Let d⁡(u,v)=0d(u,v)=0 if u=vu=v. For a given partite graph GG, we say a nonedge u​vuv is admissible if u,vu,v lie in different parts of GG.

Given graphs GG and FF, we say a subgraph HH of GG is FF-saturated relative to GG, if HH does not contain any copy of FF but the addition of any edge ee in E⁡(G)\E⁡(H)E(G)\backslash E(H) would create a copy of FF. The saturation number of FF relative to GG is denoted by

s​a​t​(G,F)=min⁡{e⁡(H):H​is​F​-saturated relative to ​G}.sat(G,F)=\min\{e(H):H\;\text{is}\;F\text{-saturated relative to }G\}\,.

Let S​a​t​(G,F)={H:H​is​F​-saturated relative to ​G​ and ​e​(H)=s​a​t​(G,F)}Sat(G,F)=\{H:H\;\text{is}\;F\text{-saturated relative to }G\text{ and }e(H)=sat(G,F)\}. If G=KnG=K_{n}, we abbreviate s​a​t​(G,F)sat(G,F) as s​a​t​(n,F)sat(n,F). The first saturation problem was studied in 1964 by Erdős, Hajnal and Moon [4] who proved that s​a​t​(n,Kr)=(r−2)​(n−1)−(r−2)​(r−1)2sat(n,K_{r})=(r-2)(n-1)-\frac{(r-2)(r-1)}{2}. For readers interested in saturation problem, we refer to the survey [3].

Finding cycle saturation number s​a​t​(n,Ck)sat(n,C_{k}) is an interesting problem in extremal graph theory. The saturation number s​a​t​(n,C3)sat(n,C_{3}) is given in [4] mentioned above. Ollmann [14] and Tuza [17] determined s​a​t​(n,C4)=⌊3​n−52⌋sat(n,C_{4})=\lfloor\frac{3n-5}{2}\rfloor for n≥5n\geq 5. Fisher, Fraughnaugh and Langley [6] derived an upper bound of s​a​t​(n,C5)sat(n,C_{5}) and was confirmed to be the exactly value of s​a​t​(n,C5)sat(n,C_{5}) by Chen [1, 2] later, that is s​a​t​(n,C5)=⌈10​(n−1)7⌉sat(n,C_{5})=\lceil\frac{10(n-1)}{7}\rceil for n≥21n\geq 21. Gould, Luczak, Schmitt [10] and Zhang, Luo, Shigeno [18] proved that ⌈7​n6⌉−2≤s​a​t​(n,C6)≤⌊3​n−32⌋\lceil\frac{7n}{6}\rceil-2\leq sat(n,C_{6})\leq\lfloor\frac{3n-3}{2}\rfloor for n≥9n\geq 9. Recently Lan, Shi, Wang and Zhang [13] showed that s​a​t​(n,C6)=43​n+O⁡(1)sat(n,C_{6})=\frac{4}{3}n+O(1) as n≥9n\geq 9. For k≥7k\geq 7, Füredi and Kim [8] showed that (1+1k+2)​n−1≤s​a​t​(n,Ck)≤(1+1k−4)+(k−42)\left(1+\frac{1}{k+2}\right)n-1\leq sat(n,C_{k})\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{k-4}\right)+\binom{k-4}{2} for n≥2​k−5n\geq 2k-5.

Another interesting problem is the partite saturation number, that is to determine s​a​t​(G,F)sat(G,F) for different FF where GG is a partite graph. Let Kk×nK_{k\times n} be the complete kk-partite graph containing nn vertices in each part. We simply abbreviate s​a​t​(Kk×n,F)sat(K_{k\times n},F) as s​a​t​(n,k,F)sat(n,k,F). Note that s​a​t​(1,k,F)=s​a​t​(k,F)sat(1,k,F)=sat(k,F), the study of partite saturation number would help us to determine general saturation numbers.

Due to the structural differences between bipartite and multipartite graphs (while studying saturation number), we only consider multipartite graph in this paper. Sullivan and Wenger [16] determined the bounds of s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,n3,Kℓ,m,p)sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}},K_{\ell,m,p}) for ℓ≥m≥p\ell\geq m\geq p and n1,n2,n3n_{1},n_{2},n_{3} sufficiently large. Moreover, they gave the exact value of s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,n3,Kℓ,ℓ,p)sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}},K_{\ell,\ell,p}) when p=ℓ,ℓ−1p=\ell,\ell-1. He and Lu [11] determined the exact value of s​a​t​(Kn1,n2,n3,t​Kℓ,ℓ,ℓ)sat(K_{n_{1},n_{2},n_{3}},tK_{\ell,\ell,\ell}) for t,ℓ≥1t,\ell\geq 1 and n1,n2,n3n_{1},n_{2},n_{3} sufficiently large. Ferrara, Jacobson, Pfender and Wenger [5] determined s​a​t​(n,k,K3)sat(n,k,K_{3}) for n≥100n\geq 100. Roberts [15] showed that s​a​t​(n,4,K4)=18​n−21sat(n,4,K_{4})=18n-21 for sufficiently large nn. Girão, Kittipassorn and Popielarz [9] determined s​a​t​(n,k,Kr)sat(n,k,K_{r}) for k≥r≥3k\geq r\geq 3 and sufficiently large nn.

In this paper we focus on determining the saturation number of cycle-saturated multipartite graphs s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1}). Since [5, 9, 16] have proved that s​a​t​(n,k,C3)=3​(k−1)​n−6sat(n,k,C_{3})=3(k-1)n-6 for large nn, we only consider Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-saturated kk-partite graph where ℓ,k≥3\ell,k\geq 3. An easy observation on a cycle-saturated multipartite graph GG is that GG must be connected. Otherwise, the addition of two vertices from different connected components and different parts of GG would not form a cycle, a contradiction. Our first results are the general bounds of s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1}).

Theorem 1.1.

For any ℓ,k≥3\ell,k\geq 3 and n≥ℓ+1kn\geq\frac{\ell+1}{k}, we have s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)≥k​nsat(n,k,C_{\ell+1})\geq kn.

Proof. Since a cycle-saturated multipartite graph must be connected, we have s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)≥k​n−1sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1})\geq kn-1. Let GG be a Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-saturated kk-partite graph with e⁡(G)=s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)e(G)=sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1}). If e⁡(G)=k​n−1e(G)=kn-1, then GG is a tree. If there exists u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) such that uu has two neighbours v,wv,w lie in different parts, then G+v​wG+vw has only a C3=u​v​w​uC_{3}=uvwu which implies GG is not Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-saturated. Thus the neighbours of any vertex u∈V⁡(G)u\in V(G) must lie in the same part which shows that GG is bipartite, a contradiction with k≥3k\geq 3. Hence we have e⁡(G)≥k​ne(G)\geq kn. ∎

Theorem 1.2.

For any ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3, ℓ≥5\ell\geq 5 and n≥⌊ℓ−12⌋n\geq\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\rfloor, we have

s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)\displaystyle sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1}) ≤k​n−ℓ+⌊ℓ−12⌋2+2​(ℓ−2​⌊ℓ−12⌋)​⌊ℓ−12⌋\displaystyle\leq\;kn-\ell+\left\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\right\rfloor^{2}+2\left(\ell-2\left\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\right\rfloor\right)\left\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\right\rfloor
={k​n+(ℓ−12)2−1,ℓ​ is odd;k​n+(ℓ−22)2+ℓ−4,ℓ​ is even.\displaystyle=\left\{\;\begin{aligned} &kn+\left(\frac{\ell-1}{2}\right)^{2}-1\,,&\;&\ell\text{ is odd}\,;\\ &kn+\left(\frac{\ell-2}{2}\right)^{2}+\ell-4\,,&\;&\ell\text{ is even}\,.\end{aligned}\right.

Theorem 1.2 gives the upper bound of s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1}) for all ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3 except 4≥ℓ≥k≥34\geq\ell\geq k\geq 3. The results below show the exact value of remaining cases. In [16] the authors gave an easy proof on s​a​t​(n,3,C4)sat(n,3,C_{4}). In this paper we give a structural proof of s​a​t​(n,3,C4)sat(n,3,C_{4}), not only show the exact value of it but also show that the extremal graph of s​a​t​(n,3,C4)sat(n,3,C_{4}) is Ω(4,3)\Omega^{(4,3)}, where Ω(4,3)\Omega^{(4,3)} would be defined in Section 2.

Theorem 1.3.

For any n≥2n\geq 2, we have

s​a​t​(n,3,C4)=3​n,S​a​t​(K3×n,C4)=Ω(4,3).sat(n,3,C_{4})=3n\,,\quad Sat(K_{3\times n},C_{4})=\Omega^{(4,3)}.
Theorem 1.4.

For any n≥2n\geq 2, we have sat(n,3,C5)={ 6,n=2, 3​n+1,n≥3.sat(n,3,C_{5})=\left\{\begin{matrix}\;6\,,\quad\quad\;&\quad n=2\,,\\ \;3n+1\,,&\quad n\geq 3\,.\end{matrix}\right.

Theorem 1.5.

For any n≥10n\geq 10, we have s​a​t​(n,4,C5)=4​n+2sat(n,4,C_{5})=4n+2.

Theorem 1.3 shows that the bounds in Theorem 1.1 are tight when ℓ=k=3\ell=k=3. All theorems above give the immediate Corollary below.

Corollary 1.1.

For any fixed ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3, we have

s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)=k​n+O⁡(ℓ2),sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1})=kn+O(\ell^{2})\,,

as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty.

For k≥3k\geq 3 and ℓ\ell is much greater than kk, we found a better construction in order to prove that s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)=k​n+O⁡(ℓ)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1})=kn+O(\ell).

Theorem 1.6.

For any fixed k≥4k\geq 4, ℓ≥60​k+11\ell\geq 60k+11 and nn sufficeintly large, we have

s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)≤k⁡(n−1)+6​⌈ℓ+15⌉.sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1})\leq k(n-1)+6\,\left\lceil\,\frac{\ell+1}{5}\,\right\rceil\,.

Moreover, we have s​a​t​(n,3,Cℓ+1)≤3​n+13​⌈ℓ+15⌉sat(n,3,C_{\ell+1})\leq 3n+13\,\lceil\,\frac{\ell+1}{5}\,\rceil while n,ℓn,\ell satisfy the same condition.

We use d​i​a​mp​(G)diam_{p}(G) to denote the maximum distance between two vertices not lie in the same part of GG. If GG is Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-saturated then d​i​a​mp​(G)≤ℓdiam_{p}(G)\leq\ell, otherwise the addition of an admissible nonedge u​vuv with d⁡(u,v)=d​i​a​mp​(G)d(u,v)=diam_{p}(G) can only create cycles with length greater than ℓ+1\ell+1.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we construct saturated subgraphs of Kk×nK_{k\times n}. We also prove Theorems 1.2 and 1.6 in this Section. In Section 3, we prove Theorem 1.3. In Section 4, we prove Theorems 1.4 and 1.5. Finally, we conclude the paper in Section 5 with some open problems.

2 Constructions of saturated subgraphs of Kk×nK_{k\times n}

In this section, we construct several graph families to show the upper bounds of our saturation results, and prove the lower bounds. We begin from a simple proposition.

Proposition 2.1.

Let G=V1∪⋯∪VkG=V_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k} be a kk-partite graph and A⊆V⁡(G)A\subseteq V(G). Let x1,…,xk∈Ax_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in A. For any different i,j∈[k]i,j\in[k], we assume the following conditions hold:
(1) for any ui∈Vi∖Au_{i}\in V_{i}\setminus A, N⁡(ui)={xi}N(u_{i})=\{x_{i}\}, and for any x∈A∖(Vi∪{xi})x\in A\setminus(V_{i}\cup\{x_{i}\}), there exists a PℓP_{\ell} connecting xx and xix_{i};
(2) there exists a Pℓ−1P_{\ell-1} connecting xix_{i} and xjx_{j};
(3) G⁡[A]G[A] is Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-saturated.
Then GG is Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-saturated.

Proof. Obviously, GG is Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-free. By (3), we only need to consider an admissible nonedge who has at least one endpoint in V⁡(G)∖AV(G)\setminus A. Let ui​wu_{i}w be an admissible nonedge with ui∈Vi∖Au_{i}\in V_{i}\setminus A, where i∈[k]i\in[k]. If w∈Vj∖Aw\in V_{j}\setminus A for some j∈[k]∖{i}j\in[k]\setminus\{i\}, by (1) and (2), there exists a Pℓ+1P_{\ell+1} connecting uiu_{i} and ww. If w∈Aw\in A, then w∉Viw\notin V_{i}. By (1), there exists a Pℓ+1P_{\ell+1} connecting uiu_{i} and ww. Hence G+ui​wG+u_{i}w would create a Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1} in each case. Thus GG is Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-saturated. ∎

2.1 Construction I

We first construct a graph family γ(ℓ,k)\gamma^{(\ell,k)}. Let G=V1∪⋯∪VkG=V_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{k} be a kk-partite graph and x1,…,xk∈V⁡(G)x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in V(G). We call (x1,…,xk)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) a good pair of GG if they do not lie in the same part of GG, that is there is no i∈[k]i\in[k] such that x1,…,xk∈Vix_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in V_{i}.

Definition 2.1.

Let ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3.
(1) If ℓ≤4\ell\leq 4 and (ℓ,k)≠(4,3)(\ell,k)\neq(4,3), let γ(3,3)=K3\gamma^{(3,3)}=K_{3}, γ(4,4)=K4\gamma^{(4,4)}=K_{4}.
(2) If ℓ≥5\ell\geq 5, let

γ(ℓ,k)=K⌊ℓ−12⌋,⌊ℓ−12⌋,(ℓ−2​⌊ℓ−12⌋)={Kℓ−12,ℓ−12,1,ℓ​ is odd,Kℓ−22,ℓ−22,2,ℓ​ is even.\gamma^{(\ell,k)}=K_{\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\rfloor\,,\,\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\rfloor\,,\,\left(\ell-2\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\rfloor\right)}=\left\{\begin{aligned} &K_{\frac{\ell-1}{2},\frac{\ell-1}{2},1}\,,&\;&\ell\text{ is odd}\,,\\ &K_{\frac{\ell-2}{2},\frac{\ell-2}{2},2}\,,&\;&\ell\text{ is even}\,.\end{aligned}\right.

Not difficult to see that any pairs of vertices u,vu,v in γ(ℓ,k)\gamma^{(\ell,k)} are connected by PℓP_{\ell} and Pℓ−1P_{\ell-1} for (ℓ,k)≠(4,3)(\ell,k)\neq(4,3) and γ(ℓ,k)\gamma^{(\ell,k)} is Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}-saturated. Since ℓ≥k\ell\geq k, the good pair of γ(ℓ,k)\gamma^{(\ell,k)} exits. The next lemma could help us to construct Ω(ℓ+1,k)\Omega^{(\ell+1,k)}.

Lemma 2.1.

For ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3 and (ℓ,k)≠(4,3)(\ell,k)\neq(4,3), let (x1,…,xk)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) be a good pair of γ(ℓ,k)\gamma^{(\ell,k)}. Then there exists a bijection f:{x1,…,xk}→[k]f\,:\,\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}\rightarrow[k] such that f⁡(xi)≠π⁡(xi)f(x_{i})\neq\pi(x_{i}), where π⁡(xi)\pi(x_{i}) is the part of γ(ℓ,k)\gamma^{(\ell,k)} containing xix_{i}.

Proof. Assume that the number of parts containing x1,…,xkx_{1},\ldots,x_{k} is rr. Then r≥2r\geq 2. Assume, without loss of generality, that xi∈Vix_{i}\in V_{i} for i∈[r]i\in[r], and xj∈V1∪⋯∪Vrx_{j}\in V_{1}\cup\cdots\cup V_{r} for j∈[k]∖[r]j\in[k]\setminus[r]. Denote

f⁡(x1)=r,\displaystyle f(x_{1})=r\,,
f(xi)=i−1,i=2,…,r,\displaystyle f(x_{i})=i-1\,,\;\,i=2,\ldots,r\,,
f(xj)=j,j=r+1,…,k.\displaystyle f(x_{j})=j\,,\;\,j=r+1,\ldots,k\,.

It is easy to check that ff satisfies the property. ∎

Definition 2.2.

For n≥⌊ℓ−12⌋n\geq\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\rfloor, ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3 and (ℓ,k)≠(4,3)(\ell,k)\neq(4,3), let W(ℓ+1,k)W^{(\ell+1,k)} be a graph satisfies the following properties:
(i) W(ℓ+1,k)W^{(\ell+1,k)} is a kk-partite graph such that each part of W(ℓ+1,k)W^{(\ell+1,k)} has exactly nn vertices.
(ii) V⁡(W(ℓ+1,k))=A∪BV(W^{(\ell+1,k)})=A\cup B with A∩B=∅A\cap B=\emptyset, W(ℓ+1,k)​[A]=γ(ℓ,k)W^{(\ell+1,k)}[A]=\gamma^{(\ell,k)} and W(ℓ+1,k)​[B]W^{(\ell+1,k)}[B] is an empty graph.
(iii) for any vertex v∈Bv\in B, dW(ℓ+1,k)​(v)=1d_{W^{(\ell+1,k)}}(v)=1, N⁡(v)⊆{x1,…,xk}N(v)\subseteq\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}, where (x1,…,xk)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}) is a good pair of W(ℓ+1,k)​[A]W^{(\ell+1,k)}[A]. For different u,v∈Bu,v\in B, if u,vu,v lie in the same part of W(ℓ+1,k)W^{(\ell+1,k)}, then N⁡(u)=N⁡(v)N(u)=N(v); otherwise N⁡(u)∩N⁡(v)=∅N(u)\cap N(v)=\emptyset.

Definition 2.2(iii) can be written as a connecting function f:{x1,…,xk}→2Bf:\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}\rightarrow 2^{B} satisfies ⋃i=1kf⁡(xi)=B\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{k}f(x_{i})=B, f⁡(xi)=Vm∩Bf(x_{i})=V_{m}\cap B for some mm, and f⁡(xi)∩f⁡(xj)=∅f(x_{i})\cap f(x_{j})=\emptyset for all i≠ji\neq j. Since W(ℓ+1,k)W^{(\ell+1,k)} is a kk-partite graph, Lemma 2.1 guarantees that such ff exists. For a bipartite graph H=A∪BH=A\cup B, we say HH is perfect to AA if for any vertex u∈Au\in A, dH​(u)≥1d_{H}(u)\geq 1; otherwise HH is non-perfect to AA.

Let G∈S​a​t​(K3×n,C4)G\in Sat(K_{3\times n},C_{4}), we write G=V1∪V2∪V3G=V_{1}\cup V_{2}\cup V_{3}. It is easy to check that W(4,3)W^{(4,3)} (Figure 1) is a C4C_{4}-saturated tripartite graph. Thus e⁡(G)≤3​ne(G)\leq 3n. The following lemmas show that S​a​t​(K3×n,C4)={W(4,3)}Sat(K_{3\times n},C_{4})=\{W^{(4,3)}\}.

Lemma 3.1.

For any distinct i,j∈[3]i,j\in[3], G⁡[Vi∪Vj]G\,[\,V_{i}\cup V_{j}\,] has no isolated vertices a,ba,b such that a∈Via\in V_{i} and b∈Vjb\in V_{j}.

For any distinct i,j∈[3]i,j\in[3], G⁡[Vi∪Vj]G\,[\,V_{i}\cup V_{j}\,] is perfect to either ViV_{i} or VjV_{j}.

For any distinct i,j∈[3]i,j\in[3], e⁡(G⁡[Vi∪Vj])=ne\left(G\,[\,V_{i}\cup V_{j}\,]\right)=n.

The next two lemmas show the core properties of GG.

Lemma 3.2.

For any distinct i,j∈[3]i,j\in[3], if G⁡[Vi∪Vj]G\,[\,V_{i}\cup V_{j}\,] is a perfect matching, then GG is not C4C_{4}-saturated.

Then for any u∈V⁡(G′)u\in V(G^{\prime}), d+​(u)=d−​(u)=1d^{+}(u)=d^{-}(u)=1. Since GG is connected, G′G^{\prime} must be a directed Hamilton cycle which can be assumed as

x1→y1→z1→x2→y2→z2→…→xn→yn→zn→x1x_{1}\rightarrow y_{1}\rightarrow z_{1}\rightarrow x_{2}\rightarrow y_{2}\rightarrow z_{2}\rightarrow\ldots\rightarrow x_{n}\rightarrow y_{n}\rightarrow z_{n}\rightarrow x_{1}

5 Concluding remark

Determining the value of s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1}) for ℓ,k≥3\ell,k\geq 3 is an interesting problem in partite saturation number. Although we have found the exact values or bounds while ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3, there is still the other half of the problem that needs to be solved urgently.

Problem 5.1.

Determine s​a​t​(n,k,Cℓ+1)sat(n,k,C_{\ell+1}) for all k>ℓ≥3k>\ell\geq 3.

The construction in this paper may not work for this case since the number of ViV_{i} containing vertices of degree 1 may strictly less than kk. But a natural upper bound can be constructed from [8] where Füredi and Kim construct graphs for s​a​t​(n,Cr)sat(n,C_{r}). If a graph GG is FF-saturated in Kk​nK_{kn} and the vertices of GG can be partitioned into balanced kk parts, then GG is a FF-saturated graph in Kk×nK_{k\times n}.

For a given graph family ℱ\mathcal{F}, a graph HH is said to be ℱ\mathcal{F}-saturated in GG if HH does not contain any copy of all graphs in ℱ\mathcal{F}, but the addition of a nonedge in E⁡(G)∖E⁡(H)E(G)\setminus E(H) would form a copy of some F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F}. Similarly we can define saturation number s​a​t​(G,ℱ)sat(G,\mathcal{F}) and partite saturation number s​a​t​(n,k,ℱ)sat(n,k,\mathcal{F}). Let 𝒞≥ℓ+1\mathcal{C}_{\geq\ell+1} be the graph families of cycles with length at least ℓ+1\ell+1, i.e. 𝒞≥ℓ+1={Cℓ+1,Cℓ+2,…}\mathcal{C}_{\geq\ell+1}=\{C_{\ell+1},C_{\ell+2},\ldots\}. Although Theorem 1.6 shows that the Construction I is not optimal, we believe that it is tight when we consider 𝒞≥ℓ+1\mathcal{C}_{\geq\ell+1}-saturation. So we have following conjecture.

Conjecture 5.1.

For ℓ≥k≥3\ell\geq k\geq 3, ℓ≥5\ell\geq 5 and sufficiently large nn,

s​a​t​(n,k,𝒞≥ℓ+1)\displaystyle sat(n,k,\mathcal{C}_{\geq\ell+1}) =k​n−ℓ+⌊ℓ−12⌋2+2​(ℓ−2​⌊ℓ−12⌋)​⌊ℓ−12⌋,\displaystyle=\;kn-\ell+\left\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\right\rfloor^{2}+2\left(\ell-2\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\rfloor\right)\left\lfloor\frac{\ell-1}{2}\right\rfloor\,,

and the extremal graphs are all in Ω(ℓ+1,k)\Omega^{(\ell+1,k)}.
